items.passage: Monitoring fishing activity on the high seas is notoriously difficult, partly because a vessel’s Automatic Identification System (AIS), which transmits its location, can simply be switched off. To estimate how often this occurs, ecologist Henri Weimerskirch and colleagues equipped 169 albatrosses with loggers that detect the radar signals of nearby ships. Comparing each vessel the birds encountered with AIS records, the researchers found that over one-third of the vessels operating in international waters of the Southern Ocean were not transmitting their locations.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It explains how researchers used seabirds to uncover the reasons many vessels in the Southern Ocean switch off their tracking systems.
It discusses a study that used seabirds to gauge how often vessels in a remote ocean region go unseen by a standard tracking system.
It describes a study showing that loggers carried by seabirds locate vessels in international waters more precisely than AIS records do.
It presents research that followed albatrosses at sea to learn how the presence of fishing vessels changes where the birds feed.
items.explanation: The text opens with a problem: a vessel’s AIS “can simply be switched off.” It then explains that the researchers equipped albatrosses with radar-detecting loggers to estimate how often this happens, and it reports the answer: “over one-third of the vessels operating in international waters of the Southern Ocean were not transmitting their locations.” Choice B states this purpose: the study used seabirds to gauge how often vessels in a remote region go unseen by a standard tracking system.

A.recipe: true first clause, invented aim (INV: motive)
A.why_wrong: The researchers did use seabirds, but the text never says why vessels switch off AIS. The study measured how often it happens, not the reasons for it.

C.why_wrong: The loggers carried by the birds did locate vessels, and the researchers compared those vessels with AIS records, but only to see whether each one was transmitting. The text never compares how precisely the two methods locate vessels.

D.recipe: right study, wrong focus (SWAP: birds as subject rather than tool)
D.why_wrong: The albatrosses were followed at sea, but in the text they serve as detectors of vessels. Nothing is said about how vessels change where the birds feed.

sources.what: Weimerskirch et al. 2020, PNAS 117(6): Ocean Sentinel; 169 wandering and Amsterdam albatrosses with loggers detecting vessel radar; in international waters more than one-third (36.9%) of vessels had no AIS operating

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine ecology, conservation). Key B. Key parts: 2 (seabirds used as the means; how often vessels go untracked). Every wrong option keeps a true first part (seabirds used; loggers locate vessels; albatrosses followed at sea) and fails on the aim or focus. Key paraphrases AIS as a standard tracking system and the Southern Ocean as a remote region.

band7.why: All three wrong options keep a true first part (seabirds used, loggers locate vessels, albatrosses followed at sea) and fail on the aim; key paraphrased (a standard tracking system, a remote ocean region). A single-finding report with no hedged second purpose, so band 6, as targeted.

items.passage:
The following text is from “The Flitting,” a poem John Clare wrote in 1832. That year, Clare relocated with his family from his native village of Helpston, England, to a cottage in neighboring Northborough.

I’ve left my own old home of homes,
Green fields and every pleasant place;
The summer like a stranger comes,
I pause and hardly know her face.
I miss the hazel’s happy green,
The blue bell’s quiet hanging blooms,
Where envy’s sneer was never seen,
Where staring malice never comes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To suggest that the speaker resents having been made to leave his village against his wishes
To express the speaker’s relief at having escaped the envy and malice of his former neighbors
To convey the speaker’s sense of estrangement after leaving a place he cherished
To describe how the countryside around the speaker’s new home differs from the landscape he left
items.explanation: The speaker says he has “left my own old home of homes” and lists what he misses there (“the hazel’s happy green, / The blue bell’s quiet hanging blooms”). Even the season feels unfamiliar: “The summer like a stranger comes, / I pause and hardly know her face.” The poem therefore conveys the speaker’s sense of estrangement after leaving a place he loved, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The speaker does miss his old home, but nothing in the lines says he was forced to leave or that he resents anyone for the move.

B.why_wrong: Envy and malice are mentioned, but as things his old home was free of: it was a place where “envy’s sneer was never seen.” He misses that place; he is not relieved to be gone.

D.why_wrong: The speaker names features of the place he left, but he never describes the countryside around his new home, so the lines draw no comparison between the two landscapes.

sources.what: text of “The Flitting” (Clare, Poems Chiefly from Manuscript, 1920 edition, Project Gutenberg #8672), copied exactly (first stanza); the editors’ introduction says these verses “were written by John Clare on June 20th, 1832, on the occasion of his moving” to the new cottage at Northborough, three miles from Helpston; the editors’ note says previously printed poems “have been brought into line with manuscript versions”
in 1832 Clare and his family moved to a larger cottage in the village of Northborough, not far from Helpston

items.notes: Area: literature (poem). Key C. First stanza copied exactly from the Gutenberg text (1920 edition, aligned with Clare's manuscripts); the source line dates the poem by its writing (1832, per the edition's introduction), not by the 1835 Rural Muse printing, whose wording may differ (that edition's introduction quotes the stanza with “mine own” and “bluebell’s”). Context sentence from Clare's biography. Hard near misses: A keeps the sense of loss and adds a cause; B turns the envy and malice of the last two lines (which describe the old home's absence of them) into relief; D keeps the list of old-home features and invents a comparison.

band7.why: Abstract feeling key (estrangement) against three partly right options (loss plus invented resentment, the envy lines reversed into relief, old-home features turned into a comparison). A plain-register lyric without a self-qualifying span, so band 6, as targeted.

fixes: source line re-dated: “John Clare’s 1835 poem” became “a poem John Clare wrote in 1832”; the text is the 1920 Gutenberg edition, whose note says printed poems were “brought into line with manuscript versions” (its own introduction quotes the stanza with “mine own” and “bluebell’s”), so the 1835 Rural Muse wording cannot be claimed; the 1832 date is the edition’s introduction (“written by John Clare on June 20th, 1832, on the occasion of his moving”)

items.passage: Economists sometimes call an incentive that ends up encouraging the very problem it targets a “cobra effect,” after an anecdote in which colonial officials in Delhi paid for dead cobras and residents began breeding the snakes. Historian Michael G. Vann observes, however, that the anecdote has never been documented. <u>Vann has examined a thoroughly documented case: in 1902, French administrators in Hanoi paid residents for every rat tail submitted, and some residents responded by severing tails and releasing the rats to reproduce.</u> Vann has accordingly proposed renaming the phenomenon the “Rat Effect.”
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It provides documentation confirming that the anecdote in the previous sentence took place, although Vann had doubted it.
It presents a recorded instance of the phenomenon, which serves as the basis for the alternative name in the last sentence.
It describes the event from which economists took the name for the phenomenon introduced in the first sentence.
It gives an example of an incentive that failed, which Vann uses to argue that economists should stop studying such incentives.
items.explanation: The first two sentences explain that the term “cobra effect” comes from an anecdote that “has never been documented.” The underlined sentence presents “a thoroughly documented case”: residents of Hanoi severed rat tails for the payment and released the rats “to reproduce,” so the incentive encouraged the problem. The last sentence then says Vann “has accordingly proposed renaming the phenomenon the ‘Rat Effect.’” The underlined sentence is a recorded instance of the phenomenon that supports the new name, as choice B says.

A.recipe: right kind of content, wrong relation (REL: confirms vs replaces)
A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence is documented, but it describes a different event, rats in Hanoi in 1902. It does not confirm the cobra anecdote, which the text says “has never been documented.”

C.recipe: partial: the job of the first sentence (PART, SWAP)
C.why_wrong: The name “cobra effect” comes from the Delhi anecdote in the first sentence, not from the Hanoi case. The Hanoi case is the source of the name Vann proposes instead.

D.why_wrong: The Hanoi payments did backfire, but Vann uses the case to propose a new name for the phenomenon, not to argue that economists should stop studying incentives.

sources.what: Great Hanoi Rat Massacre (1902): bounty per rat tail, tails cut and rats released to breed; Michael G. Vann says the cobra story cannot be proven and proposes the name Rat Effect

items.notes: Area: history and social science. Key B. Two links to the key: the underlined case is documented (contrast with the undocumented cobra anecdote) and it underlies the proposed name (“accordingly”). A and C keep part of the truth (documentation; the source of a name) and fail on the relation; D keeps “an incentive that failed” and fails on Vann's purpose.

band7.why: Key needs two links, one from the sentence after the span (“accordingly … ‘Rat Effect’”); A and D keep a true first part and fail later; C is the neighbor sentence’s job (PART). Strong band 6, as targeted.

items.passage: Wanda Gág was already an accomplished printmaker when she wrote and illustrated Millions of Cats (1928), in which an elderly man searching for a single cat returns home accompanied by an enormous procession of them. Departing from the convention of confining each illustration to its own page, Gág frequently extended a scene across two facing pages, with hand-lettered text by her brother Howard flowing through the images. The book received a Newbery Honor, an unusual distinction for a picture book, and it remains the oldest American picture book still in print.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that Gág’s experience as a printmaker was the main reason Millions of Cats became so successful
To explain how Gág and her brother divided the work of creating a picture book that later illustrators chose to imitate
To summarize the story told in a picture book and explain why that story has continued to appeal to young readers
To present a picture book that broke with a layout convention and has endured for nearly a century
items.explanation: After briefly introducing Millions of Cats and its story, the text explains that Gág “frequently extended a scene across two facing pages,” breaking with “the convention of confining each illustration to its own page.” It ends by noting the book’s Newbery Honor and that it remains “the oldest American picture book still in print.” Choice D captures both parts: the book broke with a layout convention, and it has endured for nearly a century.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions that Gág was a printmaker, but it never links that experience to the book’s success or argues for any cause of its success.

B.recipe: partial: one detail treated as the purpose, plus invented influence (PART, INV)
B.why_wrong: Howard did the hand lettering, but this is one detail of the description, and the text never says that later illustrators imitated the book.

C.recipe: true first clause, invented explanation (PART, INV)
C.why_wrong: The text does sum up the story in a clause, but it explains the book’s importance through its layout and honors, not through the appeal of its story to readers.

sources.what: Millions of Cats (1928): Gág pioneered the double-page spread; hand-lettered text by her brother; Newbery Honor 1929, one of few picture books; oldest American picture book still in print
Gág a noted printmaker; brother Howard did the hand lettering

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (children's books, illustration). Key D. Key parts: 2 (broke with a layout convention; lasting place). The source's “pioneered the double-page spread” is given as departing from the convention of one illustration per page. Each wrong option keeps a true detail (printmaker; Howard's lettering; the story) and fails on what the text does with it.

items.passage: Writing about California’s valleys and foothills in the late nineteenth century, naturalist John Muir described them as untouched wilderness, landscapes unaltered by human activity, but ecologist M. Kat Anderson argues that this description is mistaken. Drawing on historical documents and interviews with Native Californians, Anderson shows that for centuries Native peoples deliberately burned, pruned, sowed, and harvested plants throughout the region, shaping the very landscapes Muir admired. If Anderson is correct, much of what Muir saw as pristine nature more closely resembled a tended garden, and the familiar distinction between wild and cultivated land is harder to sustain than it appears.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a scholar’s research to suggest that an earlier description of a region’s landscapes failed to recognize how people had influenced them.
It discusses a scholar’s research to show that the distinction between wild and cultivated land, though valid in most regions, does not hold in California.
It describes the documents and interviews a scholar relied on in order to question whether such sources can show how Native peoples managed the land.
It traces how a scholar’s interviews with Native Californians uncovered land-management practices that Muir had closely observed and praised in his writing.
items.explanation: The text opens with Muir’s description of California’s valleys and foothills as “untouched wilderness, landscapes unaltered by human activity.” It then presents Anderson’s research showing that Native peoples “deliberately burned, pruned, sowed, and harvested plants throughout the region, shaping the very landscapes Muir admired,” and closes with a hedged conclusion: “If Anderson is correct,” much of what Muir saw as pristine “more closely resembled a tended garden.” Choice A states this purpose: the text uses the research to suggest that an earlier description of the region’s landscapes failed to recognize how people had influenced them.

B.recipe: true first clause, invented limit on the closing claim (INV, BROAD)
B.why_wrong: The text does say the distinction between wild and cultivated land “is harder to sustain than it appears,” but it never says the distinction is valid in most regions or limits its point to California, and it hedges (“If Anderson is correct”) rather than showing that the distinction fails.

C.recipe: true first clause, stance flipped on the evidence (STANCE)
C.why_wrong: The text does mention the “historical documents and interviews with Native Californians” that Anderson drew on, but it treats them as evidence for her conclusion; it never questions whether such sources are reliable.

D.recipe: true first clause, reversed later link (REV)
D.why_wrong: Anderson’s interviews did reveal Native land-management practices, but Muir did not observe or praise those practices: he admired the landscapes while describing them as “untouched wilderness, landscapes unaltered by human activity.”

sources.what: M. Kat Anderson, Tending the Wild (UC Press): challenges Muir's view of California as pristine, untouched wilderness; landscapes shaped by centuries of harvesting, tilling, sowing, pruning and burning; draws on interviews with Native Americans and historical sources

items.notes: Area: history and environmental studies. Key A. items.passage: Kathleen Booth was among the earliest programmers of the experimental computers built at Birkbeck College in London during the late 1940s. While writing all the software for a machine called the ARC2, she devised a system she called “Contracted Notation,” which represented the machine’s instructions as short symbolic codes rather than as long strings of numbers. Through later refinements and contributions by other researchers, Booth’s notation evolved into what programmers now call assembly language, a type of programming language still used to give instructions directly to a computer’s processor.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a computer scientist, describes a machine she helped construct, and then compares that machine with others built at the same time.
It introduces a computer scientist, explains why a project she worked on was abandoned, and then describes the project that replaced it.
It introduces a computer scientist, describes something she devised while working on one machine, and then traces what that work later became.
It introduces a computer scientist, describes something she devised for one machine, and then explains why others were slow to adopt it.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Booth as one of “the earliest programmers” of Birkbeck’s computers. The second describes something she created while writing software for the ARC2, “a system she called ‘Contracted Notation,’” which used short symbolic codes. The third traces its later history: “Booth’s notation evolved into what programmers now call assembly language.” Choice C follows these three moves in order.

A.recipe: first move right, second partly right, third invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text mentions the ARC2, but it describes Booth’s software for that machine rather than the machine itself, and it never compares the ARC2 with other computers.

B.recipe: first move right, later moves invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says that any of Booth’s projects was abandoned or replaced.

D.recipe: first two moves right, third reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The text says other researchers refined Booth’s notation and that it evolved into assembly language; it never says anyone was slow to adopt it.

sources.what: The Register obituary (2022): Booth wrote all the software for the ARC2 and SEC machines, inventing what she called Contracted Notation; “This language, through evolution and contributions by others, is today known as assembly language.”

items.notes: Area: history of science and technology. Key C. Three-move structure (person, work, later significance); D keeps moves 1 and 2 and breaks move 3 (adoption reversed); A keeps move 1 and bends move 2 (machine vs software) before inventing a comparison. The gloss of assembly language (symbolic codes, used to instruct the processor directly) is general knowledge, not a sourced claim.

items.passage: Once pushed to a sufficient speed, a riderless bicycle can stay upright and even recover after being knocked sideways, an ability that has often been credited either to the gyroscopic effect of the spinning front wheel or to trail, the positioning of the front wheel’s ground contact point behind the steering axis. But a team including mechanics professor Andy Ruina built a bicycle with counter-rotating disks that canceled the gyroscopic effect and with its contact point ahead of the steering axis, and the bicycle still balanced itself. Its stability, the researchers plausibly argue, can arise instead from other factors, such as the distribution of the bicycle’s mass.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes an ability of a machine, presents two common explanations for that ability, and then reports an experiment showing that the two effects must work together to produce it.
It describes an ability of a machine, explains why engineers first became interested in it, and then predicts how the researchers’ finding will change the design of bicycles.
It reports an ability of a machine, weighs several possible causes of that ability, and then calls for more research before any of those causes is accepted.
It describes an ability of a machine, uses one experiment to cast doubt on two common explanations for it, and then points to a cause that the author finds plausible.
items.explanation: The text first describes a riderless bicycle’s ability to “stay upright and even recover after being knocked sideways.” It then names two common explanations, “the gyroscopic effect” and “trail,” and describes a single experiment that undercuts both: a bicycle built without either effect “still balanced itself.” Finally, it points to another cause that the author considers reasonable: stability, “the researchers plausibly argue, can arise instead from other factors, such as the distribution of the bicycle’s mass.” Choice D describes these moves.

A.recipe: first two moves right, third reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: The text does present two common explanations, but the experiment removed both effects and the bicycle still balanced, so it does not show that the effects must work together.

B.recipe: first move right, later moves invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: The text never says why engineers became interested in bicycle stability, and it makes no prediction about future bicycle design.

C.recipe: first moves right, invented final move (INV: call for more research)
C.why_wrong: The text does consider possible causes, but it does not call for more research: it ends by pointing to a cause, the distribution of the bicycle’s mass, which it says the researchers “plausibly argue” for.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Ann Radcliffe’s 1791 novel The Romance of the Forest. La Motte has entered a ruined abbey in a forest.

La Motte paused a moment, for he felt a sensation of sublimity rising into terror—a suspension of mingled astonishment and awe! The deepening gloom now reminded La Motte that he had no time to lose; but curiosity prompted him to explore further, and he obeyed the impulse. As he walked over the broken pavement, the sound of his steps ran in echoes through the place, and seemed like the mysterious accents of the dead reproving the sacrilegious mortal who thus dared to disturb their precincts.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To convey a character’s mixed feelings of dread and fascination as he explores an eerie place
To suggest that La Motte can actually hear the voices of people who were once buried in the abbey
To show La Motte’s regret at having entered a place that others regard as sacred
To explain why La Motte decides to leave the abbey before night falls
items.explanation: La Motte feels “a sensation of sublimity rising into terror,” “a suspension of mingled astonishment and awe!” Although the gloom reminds him “that he had no time to lose,” “curiosity prompted him to explore further,” and his echoing steps seem to him like the voices of the dead. The text therefore conveys his mixed feelings of dread and fascination as he explores the ruin, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The echoes of La Motte’s own steps only “seemed like the mysterious accents of the dead.” The text does not say he hears real voices of people buried there.

C.why_wrong: The echoes seem to reprove a “sacrilegious mortal,” but this is how the sounds strike La Motte, not regret on his part, and he keeps exploring because curiosity “prompted him to explore further.”

D.why_wrong: The gloom reminds La Motte that he has little time, but he does not leave: “curiosity prompted him to explore further, and he obeyed the impulse.”

sources.what: text of The Romance of the Forest (Radcliffe, 1791), Project Gutenberg #64701, chapter 2 (abbey scene); copied exactly, one passage of two sentences omitted between the first and second sentences (adapted)

items.notes: Area: literature (Gothic novel). Key A. Adapted: the sentences “He surveyed the vastness ... reared them!” are left out between the first and second sentences; the double hyphen of the e-text is set as a closed em dash. Distractors: B literalizes the echoes, C turns the word “sacrilegious” into regret, D reverses his choice to stay.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Erckmann-Chatrian’s 1864 novel The Conscript, which is set in France in the early 1800s.

When [the Emperor Napoleon] passed through Champagne, people gathering the harvest would leave everything to run and see him; women, children, and old men would come a distance of eight or ten leagues to line his route, and cheer and cry, “Vive l’Empereur!” [Long live the Emperor!] One would think that he was a god, that mankind owed its life to him, and that, if he died, the world would crumble and be no more. A few old Republicans would shake their heads and mutter over their wine that the Emperor might yet fall, but they passed for fools.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why some people in France wanted the Emperor removed from power
To describe the hardships that the Emperor’s journeys caused for farmworkers at harvest time
To reveal that the narrator shared the old Republicans’ doubts about the Emperor’s future
To convey the extraordinary devotion that the Emperor inspired among ordinary people

items.passage: Photography is commonly regarded as an aid to memory, but psychologist Linda Henkel has found that it can impair recollection. Participants guided through an art museum were instructed to observe certain objects and to photograph others; when tested subsequently, they remembered fewer of the objects they had photographed in their entirety and recalled fewer of those objects’ details. items.passage: Until the mid-twentieth century, most scholars regarded Gullah, the language of Black communities on the Sea Islands of South Carolina and Georgia, as a substandard variety of English, a jumble of mispronunciations and grammatical errors. After extensive fieldwork in those communities, linguist Lorenzo Dow Turner concluded instead that Gullah had been strongly influenced by African languages. items.passage: From the 1920s into the 1970s, Kiowa photographer Horace Poolaw documented life in and around Mountain View, Oklahoma, producing portraits of relatives, friends, and tribal leaders and photographing the Indian fairs he attended as both spectator and official photographer. items.passage: Many students now take class notes on laptops, a habit that a widely cited 2014 study appeared to discourage: participants who wrote their notes by hand outperformed those who typed them on later tests of lecture content. But conclusions about the superiority of handwritten notes may be premature: when psychologist Kayla Morehead and colleagues repeated the 2014 experiment, some trends favored longhand, yet test performance did not consistently differ between groups—not even between students who took notes and students who took none. Pooling the results of several such repetitions, the team found only a small, statistically unreliable advantage for writing by hand.

To present research suggesting that a reported advantage of one way of taking notes is less certain than an earlier study implied
items.explanation: The text begins with a 2014 study in which students who wrote notes by hand “outperformed those who typed them,” then cautions that “conclusions about the superiority of handwritten notes may be premature.” It supports that caution with a repetition of the study in which performance “did not consistently differ between groups” and pooled results showing only “a small, statistically unreliable advantage.” Choice D states this purpose.

items.passage: Even on days without major earthquakes, seismometers detect Earth vibrating continuously at characteristic low frequencies, a phenomenon called the “hum.” The hum’s daily energy is equivalent to that of an earthquake of roughly magnitude 6, far exceeding what the numerous small earthquakes occurring each day could collectively supply. Slow, or “silent,” earthquakes have likewise been ruled out as its source in all but a few instances. Instead, a team of seismologists is likely correct that the hum originates as storm energy is converted into long ocean waves interacting with the seafloor: the team traced it primarily to the northern Pacific and the southern oceans, each during its own hemisphere’s winter.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a natural process, rejects two explanations for it, and then concludes that no explanation proposed so far is convincing.
It presents a scientific observation, considers two proposed causes that the author finds unconvincing, and then cites seasonal evidence that supports one of them.
It introduces a geophysical phenomenon, indicates that two possible sources cannot account for it, and then offers an explanation the author considers probable.
It reports a geophysical discovery, explains how scientists first detected it, and then describes a debate about whether it poses any danger.
items.explanation: The text introduces the “hum,” Earth’s continuous vibration. It then rules out two sources: “the numerous small earthquakes occurring each day” could not supply enough energy, and slow earthquakes “have likewise been ruled out.” Finally it presents a third account, that the hum arises from storm energy in the oceans, which the author says a team “is likely correct” about. A.why_wrong: The text does reject two explanations, but it then endorses a third, saying the team “is likely correct,” rather than concluding that no explanation is convincing.

B.recipe: first two moves right, third move misattached (INV)
B.why_wrong: The seasonal evidence supports the ocean-storm account, a third explanation; it does not support either of the two causes the text has already ruled out.

D.why_wrong: The text does not explain how the hum was first detected or describe any debate about danger; it weighs possible sources of the hum.

The following text is from Henry Lawson’s 1896 short story collection While the Billy Boils. The narrator describes Golden Gully, an abandoned gold-mining area in Australia.

The predominant note of the scene was a painful sense of listening, that never seemed to lose its tension—a listening as though for the sounds of digger [gold miner] life, sounds that had gone and left a void that was accentuated by the signs of a former presence. The main army of diggers had long ago vanished to new rushes, leaving only its stragglers and deserters behind. These were men who were too poor to drag families about, men who were old and feeble, and men who had lost their faith in fortune.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To convey the emptiness of a once-busy mining area and describe the miners who have stayed
To describe a battle in which an army of miners was defeated and scattered across the countryside
To show that the miners who remain in Golden Gully are content with the quiet of the deserted field
To explain why the miners who left Golden Gully later regretted their decision to search elsewhere
items.explanation: The first sentence describes the scene as “a painful sense of listening” for “sounds that had gone and left a void,” which conveys how empty the place has become. The rest of the text says most miners “had long ago vanished” and describes those left behind: men “too poor,” “old and feeble,” or who “had lost their faith in fortune.” Choice A covers both parts.

B.why_wrong: “Army,” “stragglers,” and “deserters” describe the miners figuratively; the miners left for “new rushes,” and no battle takes place.

C.why_wrong: The text calls the scene’s silence “painful” and describes the remaining men as poor, feeble, or without faith in fortune, not content.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that the main body of miners “vanished to new rushes”; it says nothing about whether they regretted leaving.

items.passage: Panther chameleons (Furcifer pardalis) can change color within minutes during courtship or contests between males. Such changes have generally been attributed to the movement of pigment-containing structures within skin cells. But a team led by physicist Jérémie Teyssier and biologist Michel Milinkovitch found that the lizards <u>shift their color by actively adjusting the spacing of a lattice of tiny guanine crystals in a layer of skin cells called iridophores</u>, which changes the wavelengths of light the skin reflects. A deeper layer of iridophores containing larger crystals reflects much of the near-infrared light in sunlight, potentially helping keep the animals cool.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the movement of pigments that researchers had long thought was responsible for the lizards’ color changes.
It explains how the lizards accomplish the color changes mentioned at the beginning of the text.
It explains how the lizards’ skin protects them from overheating in direct sunlight.
It identifies the reason that male chameleons change color more often than female chameleons do.
items.explanation: The first sentence says panther chameleons “can change color within minutes.” The underlined portion explains how they do it: they “shift their color by actively adjusting the spacing of a lattice of tiny guanine crystals.” Choice B states this function.

A.why_wrong: The pigment explanation appears in the second sentence as the earlier view; the underlined portion presents the team’s different finding.

C.why_wrong: Protection from heat is the job of the last sentence, which describes a deeper layer of iridophores; the underlined portion concerns color change.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares how often males and females change color; it mentions contests between males only as one occasion for color change.

items.notes: Area: natural science (biology and physics). Key B. The underlined span is a mechanism (as in 2.14 and 2.15). The following text is adapted from Amy Levy’s 1889 poem “Cambridge in the Long.” The speaker, who has left a busy city, is spending the summer vacation in Cambridge, an English university town.

Where drowsy sound of college-chimes
Across the air is blown,
And drowsy fragrance of the limes [linden trees],
I lie and dream alone.

This is the place; it is not strange,
But known of old and dear.—
What went I forth to seek? The change
Is mine; why am I here?

Alas, in vain I turned away,
I fled the town in vain;
The strenuous life of yesterday
Calleth me back again.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker describes a peaceful refuge and then acknowledges that it has not released the speaker from a busier life.
The speaker recalls a familiar town and then explains how the town has changed since the speaker last saw it.
The speaker describes the noise and hurry of a city and then expresses relief at having finally escaped to a calmer place.
The speaker praises the beauty of a university and then urges others to visit it during the summer.
items.explanation: The first stanza pictures a quiet scene of “drowsy” chimes and fragrance where the speaker can “lie and dream alone.” The last stanza admits, “in vain I turned away, / I fled the town in vain,” since “the strenuous life of yesterday / Calleth me back again.” Choice A describes this movement from a peaceful retreat to the admission that the retreat has not freed the speaker.

B.recipe: word hook on “The change / Is mine” (LIT)
B.why_wrong: The speaker says “The change / Is mine,” meaning that the speaker has changed; the place is “known of old and dear” and “not strange,” so the poem does not describe the town changing.

C.why_wrong: The poem begins with the calm scene, not the city, and ends by saying the escape was “in vain,” not with relief.

D.why_wrong: The speaker never addresses or urges other people; the poem is about the speaker’s own failed retreat.

sources.what: Amy Levy, A London Plane-Tree, and Other Verse (1889), poem “Cambridge in the Long”; stanzas 1, 3 and 4 copied exactly (stanza 2 left out, so 'adapted'), gloss added

items.passage: Medieval bestiaries, such as the Aberdeen Bestiary and the Ashmole Bestiary, both produced in England around 1200, describe real and imaginary creatures indiscriminately and pair each animal with a Christian moral lesson, relying largely on earlier texts rather than on direct observation. But not every medieval treatment of animals depended on inherited authority. In the 1240s, Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II composed De arte venandi cum avibus (The Art of Hunting with Birds), a treatise that undertakes to describe birds as they actually are, reports experiments such as covering vultures’ eyes to determine whether they hunt by smell, and frequently contradicts Aristotle.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It compares two English manuscripts and then traces how their illustrations influenced a later book about falconry.
It describes two medieval books about animals and then argues that the moral lessons in such books rested on careful observation of nature.
It summarizes the history of falconry in medieval Europe and then describes a ruler’s efforts to protect certain birds.
It characterizes a kind of medieval book through two examples and then describes a work from the same period with a different approach.
items.explanation: The first sentence characterizes medieval bestiaries, naming “the Aberdeen Bestiary and the Ashmole Bestiary,” as books “relying largely on earlier texts rather than on direct observation.” The text then says “not every medieval treatment of animals depended on inherited authority” and describes Frederick II’s treatise, which “undertakes to describe birds as they actually are.” Choice D follows this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text does not compare the two bestiaries with each other or mention their illustrations or any influence on Frederick II’s book.

B.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)
B.why_wrong: The text does describe two bestiaries, but it says they relied on earlier texts “rather than on direct observation”; observation is what sets Frederick II’s book apart.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no history of falconry, and Frederick II’s treatise is described as a study of birds, not an effort to protect them.

Bestiary (Wikipedia): each beast paired with a moral lesson; compilations of earlier texts; no distinction between existing and imaginary animals; Aberdeen Bestiary (12th century) and Ashmole Bestiary (early 13th century, England)

items.passage: Because Islamic teachings prohibit drinking wine, one might expect that the Mediterranean wine trade, which had flourished under the Roman Empire, diminished in regions that subsequently came under Muslim rule. Recent chemical evidence complicates that expectation: analyzing residues preserved in more than 100 transport jars, or amphorae, dating from the fifth to the eleventh centuries, archaeologist Léa Drieu and colleagues determined that wine continued to be traded through Sicily while the island was under Islamic rule, with some exported from Palermo to ports under Christian control.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes how archaeologists identify the contents of ancient jars and then explains why that method has proved unreliable.
It presents an assumption that might seem reasonable and then describes recent findings that call it into question.
It presents two conflicting accounts of Sicily’s history and then describes a discovery that confirmed one of them.
It describes an expectation about trade under Muslim rule and then presents evidence that wine production ended in Sicily but continued elsewhere.
items.explanation: The first sentence sets out what “one might expect”: that the wine trade “diminished in regions that subsequently came under Muslim rule.” The text then says “recent chemical evidence complicates that expectation” and reports that wine “continued to be traded through Sicily while the island was under Islamic rule.” Choice B describes this structure.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template: method, then its flaw (INV)
A.why_wrong: The analysis of residues is mentioned only as how the team reached its finding; the text never says the method is unreliable.

C.recipe: wholly wrong template: conflicting accounts resolved (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text presents one expectation, not two conflicting accounts, and the finding complicates that expectation rather than confirming it.

D.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The text does open with an expectation about trade under Muslim rule, but the evidence shows that wine kept moving through Sicily, not that it stopped there.

sources.what: Drieu et al. (2021, PNAS): wine one of the most important Mediterranean commodities under the Roman Empire; less known whether trade continued under Islamic control; chemical analysis of 109 transport amphorae from the 5th to 11th centuries; wine continued to be traded through Sicily in the Islamic period, supplied locally and exported from Palermo to ports under Christian control; trade included products prohibited by the hadiths

items.passage: Old collections of birds’ eggs are sometimes dismissed as relics of an outdated hobby, but they deserve better. items.passage: Helen Cordero was a potter from Cochiti Pueblo in New Mexico who, in 1964, created her first Storyteller figure: a clay grandfather surrounded by five small children, inspired partly by her own grandfather, Santiago Quintana. Her later Storytellers frequently feature numerous children clambering onto the central figure to listen. Cordero collected her own clay near Cochiti and prepared her own paints from clay and plants, and she shaped each child separately, which allowed her to vary its position on the larger figure.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a disagreement between two potters and then explains how it was settled.
It introduces an artist and then describes some features of her work.
It compares two styles of pottery and then argues that one is more traditional.
It explains why a type of clay figure became less popular and then describes efforts to revive it.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Cordero as “a potter from Cochiti Pueblo” and names her first Storyteller figure. The rest of the text describes those figures, including the “numerous children clambering onto the central figure,” and how she “shaped each child separately.” Choice B describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions only one potter and no disagreement.

C.why_wrong: The text describes one artist’s work; it does not compare styles or argue that one is more traditional.

D.why_wrong: The text never says the figures became less popular or needed to be revived.

sources.what: Helen Cordero (Wikipedia): lifelong resident of Cochiti Pueblo; Storyteller design in 1964, a male figure surrounded by five grandchildren, partly inspired by her grandfather Santiago Quintana; later Storytellers with many children climbing on him; dug her own clay and prepared her own pigments from clay and plant materials; made the children separately to vary their placement

items.notes: Area: arts (pottery). Key B. As in 1.13 and 1.19, every distractor is a wholly different template, the easy-tier pattern.

items.passage: After the phonograph was invented in 1877, researchers began transporting the machines into the field to record songs and stories that communities had preserved through memory rather than writing. In 1890, anthropologist Jesse Walter Fewkes recorded Passamaquoddy songs, legends, and stories in Maine on 36 wax cylinders. Beginning in 1906, composer Percy Grainger used a phonograph to document folk singers in Lincolnshire, England, and composers Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály eventually recorded hundreds of cylinders of traditional melodies in Hungarian villages.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text describes a disagreement among composers, then explains how it was resolved.
The text explains how the phonograph worked, then compares it with later recording devices.
The text describes a new practice, then gives several examples of it.
The text presents a problem with early recordings, then describes efforts to restore them.
items.explanation: The first sentence describes a general development: researchers “began transporting the machines into the field to record songs and stories.” The next three sentences give examples: Fewkes in Maine, Grainger in Lincolnshire, and Bartók and Kodály in Hungary. Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text names several composers but describes no disagreement among them.

B.why_wrong: The text does not explain how the phonograph worked or mention later recording devices.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about damaged recordings or efforts to restore them.

sources.what: Library of Congress blog (Now See Hear!, 2023): Jesse Walter Fewkes borrowed a cylinder recording device from Thomas Edison in 1890 and traveled to Maine to record the Passamaquoddy community, recording 36 cylinders of songs, legends, stories and linguistic terms
Percy Grainger used a phonograph from 1906, starting at Brigg in Lincolnshire, more than 200 Edison cylinder recordings of folk singers
Bartók and Kodály recorded hundreds of cylinders; in 1908 they traveled into the countryside to collect old Hungarian folk melodies

items.notes: Area: humanities and history (music, ethnography). Key C. Same moves as 1.12 (a general situation, then specific examples), in new words; every distractor is a wholly different template. The 'oldest surviving field recordings' claim about Fewkes is left out because the fetched pages do not state it.

items.passage: Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight and intensifies what is known as the urban heat island effect, in which cities become considerably hotter than the surrounding countryside. Hoping to reduce this heat on city streets, officials in Los Angeles, California, began in 2017 to coat selected streets with CoolSeal, a gray sealant that reflects more sunlight than conventional black asphalt does. The coating costs approximately $40,000 per mile and lasts for seven years, and early measurements indicated that the surface of coated pavement was about 10°F cooler than that of nearby uncoated pavement.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe a city’s effort to cool its streets and the early results
To argue that other cities should coat their streets with the same material
To compare the costs of several methods for lowering temperatures in cities
To explain why asphalt makes cities hotter than the surrounding countryside
items.explanation: The text explains that Los Angeles officials were “hoping to reduce this heat on city streets,” describes the coating they began applying in 2017, and reports that “the surface of coated pavement was about 10°F cooler” than that of uncoated pavement. Choice A states this purpose: an effort and its early results.

B.recipe: stance the text does not take (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: The text reports what Los Angeles did but never says other cities should do the same.

C.why_wrong: The text gives the cost of only one method, the coating.

D.why_wrong: Only the first sentence explains why asphalt makes cities hotter; the rest of the text is about the city’s response.

sources.what: Green Building Advisor, 'Los Angeles Lightens Streets in Bid to Stay Cool' (2017): heat island effect; CoolSeal, a gray-colored sealer that lowers road temperatures; city applying a reflective coating to some streets from May 2017; coated pavement surface 10 F cooler than an adjacent uncoated area; costs $40,000 a mile and lasts seven years

items.notes: Area: social science (urban policy). Key A, worded away from 1.8's 'an effort ... and some results of that effort'. Later research questioning the coating's effect on people's comfort is not part of this item.

items.passage: When a predator approaches, many animals flee, conceal themselves, or fight back. Others respond more unexpectedly: they stop moving and remain motionless, as if they were dead. <u>This behavior is known as thanatosis.</u> Although thanatosis may seem risky, it can improve an animal’s chances of survival. Biologist Takahisa Miyatake and colleagues investigated this possibility using red flour beetles, selectively breeding, over ten generations, one population that feigned death for long periods and another that did so only briefly. When a jumping spider was introduced, beetles from the long-feigning population were captured less frequently.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why some predators ignore prey that remains still.
It describes the result of an experiment involving red flour beetles.
It presents a hypothesis that the study discussed later fails to support.
It provides the name of a behavior that the rest of the text examines.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined one describes animals that “stop moving and remain motionless, as if they were dead.” The underlined sentence gives this behavior a name, “thanatosis,” and the rest of the text uses that term while describing a study of the behavior in beetles. Choice D states this function.

A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence only names the behavior; the text never explains why predators might ignore still prey.

B.recipe: the job of a later sentence (PART)
B.why_wrong: The experiment’s result is given in the last sentence, not in the underlined one.

C.why_wrong: The underlined sentence names a behavior rather than proposing a hypothesis, and the study described later supports the idea that the behavior can improve an animal’s chances of survival.

sources.what: Miyatake et al. (2004, Proceedings of the Royal Society B): death-feigning (thanatosis) in red flour beetles; two-way artificial selection for duration over 10 generations; predation by an Adanson jumping spider was lower among beetles from long-duration strains

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Key D, worded away from 1.11's key. The term is introduced without 1.11's 'Scientists call this process' frame. Distractors: A invented, B a later sentence's job, C a sibling label (REL).
